before:
You were not at fault. You got your car repaired at a certified body shop. The paint matches, the panels line up, and everything looks fine on the surface. But try to sell or trade in that vehicle, and you will quickly learn something frustrating: it is worth less than it was before the crash. A repaired car carries a permanent accident history that shows up on Carfax and AutoCheck reports, and buyers know it. That lost value is real money — and in both Georgia and South Carolina, you have the right to recover it from the at-fault driver's insurance company.

This is called a diminished value claim, and it is one of the most overlooked forms of compensation after a car accident. Thousands of drivers across both states never file one because they do not know the claim exists or the insurance company never mentions it. As the Cornell Law Institute explains, an injured party is entitled to full compensation for all losses caused by the tortfeasor — including the reduction in vehicle market value.

You were not at fault. You got your car repaired at a certified body shop. The paint matches, the panels line up, and everything looks fine on the surface. But try to sell or trade in that vehicle, and you will quickly learn something frustrating: it is worth less than it was before the crash. A repaired car carries a permanent accident history that can show up on Carfax and AutoCheck reports, and buyers know it. That lost value is real money — and in both Georgia and South Carolina, you have the right to recover it from the at-fault driver, whose liability insurer handles the claim.

This is called a diminished value claim, and it is one of the most overlooked forms of compensation after a car accident. As the Legal Information Institute at Cornell Law School explains, a tort victim can recover compensatory damages for all types of losses, including property damage.

before: This is the most common type and the one most courts recognize. Inherent diminished value refers to the stigma loss your car suffers simply because it has been in an accident. No matter how perfect the repair, a buyer looking at two identical vehicles will pay less for the one with a crash on its record. This loss exists regardless of repair quality.
after: This is the most common type and the one most disputes are about. Inherent diminished value refers to the stigma loss your car suffers simply because it has been in an accident. No matter how perfect the repair, a buyer looking at two identical vehicles will pay less for the one with a crash on its record. This loss exists regardless of repair quality.

before:
Many insurers rely on what is called the "17c formula," named after a State Farm claims manual section. It works like this: take your car's pre-accident value from NADA or a similar guide, multiply it by 10% (the maximum they will acknowledge as diminished value), then apply a series of multipliers that reduce the number based on the car's mileage and the severity of damage.

The problem with 17c is that it almost always undervalues your claim. The 10% cap is arbitrary. A two-year-old SUV with frame damage can easily lose 20-30% of its value, but the 17c formula would never get you there. Courts in both Georgia and South Carolina have rejected this formula as the sole measure of diminished value.
after:
Many insurers rely on what is called the "17c formula," named after paragraph 17(c) of an injunction entered after Mabry in the Georgia class action Walker v. American National General Insurance Co., as the Georgia Court of Appeals explained in Amica Mutual Insurance Co. v. Sanders (2015). It is an insurance-industry formula, not law. It works like this: take your car's pre-accident value from NADA or a similar guide, multiply it by 10% (the maximum they will acknowledge as diminished value), then apply a series of multipliers that reduce the number based on the car's mileage and the severity of damage.

The problem with 17c is that it almost always undervalues your claim. The 10% cap is arbitrary. The formula also discounts for mileage that book value already reflects, and it involves no inspection of the repaired car. Georgia's Insurance Commissioner has told insurers that the Department has never endorsed any formula and that total reliance on one formula may not be appropriate (Directive 08-P&C-2).

before:
A qualified independent appraiser examines the vehicle's pre-accident value, the nature and extent of damage, the quality of repairs, and comparable sales data to determine the actual market value loss. This approach uses real-world data rather than an insurance company formula designed to minimize payouts.

Independent appraisals typically cost $250 to $500 but routinely support figures three to five times what the 17c formula produces. For vehicles involved in serious collisions — including motorcycle accidents with major frame damage — an independent appraisal is essential.

before:
The Georgia Court of Appeals decision in State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co. v. Mabry (274 Ga. App. 103, 2005) fundamentally changed the diminished value landscape. The court held that first-party diminished value claims are valid under Georgia's uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage provisions. If the at-fault driver's insurance does not adequately cover your diminished value, you can pursue a claim under your own UM/UIM policy.

Before Mabry, insurers routinely denied first-party diminished value claims. After the ruling, Georgia became arguably the strongest state in the country for these claims.

Bad Faith Protections Under O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6

Georgia law provides additional teeth through its bad faith statute. Under O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6, if an insurance company refuses to pay a valid claim without reasonable cause, the policyholder can recover a penalty of up to 50% of the claim amount, plus reasonable attorney's fees. This provision gives insurers a strong incentive to negotiate diminished value claims in good faith rather than stonewalling.
after:
The Supreme Court of Georgia's decision in State Farm Mutual Automobile Insurance Co. v. Mabry (274 Ga. 498, 556 S.E.2d 114 (2001)) fundamentally changed the diminished value landscape. The court held that when your own auto policy promises to pay for "loss to your car," the insurer must pay for any loss in value the repairs do not restore — and must assess diminished value on every collision or comprehensive claim, without a separate request.

Before Mabry, State Farm did not assess diminished value unless a policyholder asked. After it, Georgia's Insurance Commissioner directed every property and casualty insurer to assess diminished value on first-party physical-damage claims, and Georgia became arguably the strongest state in the country for these claims.

Bad Faith Protections Under O.C.G.A. §§ 33-4-6 and 33-4-7

Georgia law provides additional teeth through its bad faith statutes. O.C.G.A. § 33-4-7 requires the at-fault driver's insurer to adjust property-damage claims fairly and promptly and, where liability is reasonably clear, to make a good-faith effort to settle. If it refuses a demand to settle for a specific amount — sent by certified mail or statutory overnight delivery — for 60 days, and you later recover at least that amount in court, it can owe a penalty of up to 50% of the loss or $5,000, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6 provides a similar penalty against your own insurer after a 60-day demand. These provisions give insurers a strong incentive to negotiate diminished value claims in good faith rather than stonewalling, though an insurer's use of the 17c formula is not by itself bad faith (Amica, 2015).

before: If another driver caused the accident, you can pursue a diminished value claim against their liability insurance. South Carolina courts have consistently recognized diminished value as a legitimate component of property damage. Under S.C. Code § 38-77-30, liability policies must provide property damage coverage, and courts have held that diminished value falls within it.
after: If another driver caused the accident, you can pursue a diminished value claim against their liability insurance. South Carolina measures damage to a vehicle as the cost of repairs plus any remaining loss in value (Newman v. Brown, 1955), and every South Carolina liability policy must carry at least $25,000 of property-damage coverage (S.C. Code § 38-77-140). Newman involved repairs that did not fully restore the car; whether South Carolina law also reaches pure stigma loss after a proper repair has not been squarely decided.

before: Unlike Georgia, South Carolina has not broadly opened the door to first-party diminished value claims. Pursuing a claim under your own collision or UM/UIM policy is significantly harder. South Carolina courts have generally held that collision coverage pays to restore the vehicle through repairs, not to compensate for residual stigma loss. If the at-fault driver is uninsured or underinsured, your options for recovering diminished value may be limited.
after: Unlike Georgia, South Carolina has not broadly opened the door to first-party diminished value claims. In Schulmeyer v. State Farm (2003), the South Carolina Supreme Court held that a collision policy paying the lower of actual cash value or the cost of repair does not also owe diminished value once the car is properly repaired. If the at-fault driver is underinsured, your options may be limited. If the driver is uninsured, South Carolina uninsured motorist coverage includes at least $25,000 of property-damage coverage (S.C. Code § 38-77-150), but no South Carolina appellate court has addressed diminished value under it.
